newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah strengthens after rates hike.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah strengthens after rates hike.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah strengthened agianst the dollar in late trading on Tuesday after the central bank raised its bilateral SBI rates, dealers said.
They said the central bank move boosted the market as offshore fund managers were looking for good entry levels into the rupiah because of its attractive yields.

Bank Indonesia raised the rates for bilateral SBIs (central bank certificates) of maturities between one week and three months. One-week SBI rates were raised to 20 percent from 10.5, two to 22 percent from 11 percent, one-month to 30 percent from 11.625 and three to 28 percent from 11.5 percent.
It kept overnight SBIs at 15.0 percent, two-to-six day at 16.0 and six-month and one-year at 12.125 and 12.75 percent.
The rupiah closed at 2,885/2,900 against the dollar in Jakarta after falling to a historic low of 3.045. Tomorrow and today rupiah closed at 2,870/75 and 2,965/75, respectively.

Dealers said fund managers in Hong Kong attempted to lock in the high yields provided by the rupiah and started unloading dollars, pushing the rupiah up to 2,980. But local corporate buying, combined with comments by Coordinating Minister Saleh Afiff about new rules, unsettled the market and triggered a wave of dollar covering, driving the rupiah back to the 3,045 low.
Afiff said liquidity tightening was now the "homework" of the finance minister and the central bank governor.
"I cannot explain how the further tightening will be carried out. Because it will be done tomorrow (Tuesday)," he was quoted by the Bisnis Indonesia daily as saying.
However, officials at the finance ministry, the coordinating ministry and the central bank said there was no news conference scheduled for Tuesday.
Dealers said concerns about new rules caused some panic in the market as various rumours emerged and battered the rupiah.
"The tight money policy has worked so far. There is a good chance that market confidence is back," Png said.
"We saw that some corporates who wanted to cover dollars have decided to hold off," Png added.
Dealers said swap rates which rose sharply earlier had also eased in the afternoon on offshore selling.
"I think offshore players are just happy to unload because they were too high," one dealer in Singapore said.
Six-month swap jumped to a high of 448 points before easing to 350/400 points. Three-month fell to 245/275 from 300 and one-month to 180 from 200 points.
"It's unrealistically low. We don't think the rupiah would fall to 3,500 in six months time. We are just happy to supply," one dealer said.
Currency dealers said the sharp difference between the short- and longer-term rates suggested that the current instability was temporary.

"... things are starting to settle down. Certainly the rupiah at 3,000 is probably the low at the moment, and, to be honest, we are expecting it to start firming up by the end of this week and start to appreciate," Nicholas Bibby, an economist with Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, said.
Pardy Kendy, chief treasurer of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, said offshore players were trying to enter the market by selling six-month swaps and establishing short dollar positions.
"The rupiah is really undervalued at current levels," Kendy said, adding that the fall of the rupiah since January had made it one of the most undervalued currencies in the region.
The rupiah, which started the year at 2,363, had fallen more than 26 percent if the 3,045 low is taken into account.

Kendy said the Thai baht, whose weakness has triggered speculative attacks on all currencies in the region, had fallen only 25.2 percent since January followed by a 13.65 percent fall in the peso and 10.67 percent in the Malaysian ringgit.

"I'm surprised to see our rupiah has fallen more than the baht while our economy is in a better shape. The rupiah is really overshooting," he said, adding foreign players seemed to detect the undervaluation and tried to lock in the high yields.

Kendy said offshore fund managers were seen selling dollars in the spot market and placing the rupiah they obtained in six-month swaps, effectively depositing money in rupiah to take advantage of high interest rates.
